statement: A chocolate bar has 3 rows with 4 squares in each row. Ana eats half of the bar. Then Bo eats a quarter of the whole bar. How many squares are left?

choices.misconception: I thought a quarter always means 4 squares, so I took away 6 and then 4.
I counted the bar as 4 rows of 4 squares, so I started with 16 instead of 12.
I took away Ana's half and forgot about Bo.
I found how many squares were eaten, not how many are left.

hints: Count all the squares in the bar first.
Find the whole, then find half of it and a quarter of it. Both fractions are of the whole bar, so work them out from the same total and take both away.
The bar has 12 squares. Half of 12 is 6, and a quarter of 12 is 3. Take both away from 12.

solutions.reliable: The bar has $3 \times 4 = 12$ squares. Ana eats half: 6 squares. Bo eats a quarter of the whole bar: 3 squares. That is $6 + 3 = 9$ eaten, so $12 - 9 = 3$ squares are left. The idea to keep: find the whole first, then each fraction of it.
solutions.elegant: Half and a quarter make three quarters, so one quarter is left. A quarter of 12 is 3.

whyOnTest: Two fractions of the same whole must both be taken from that whole, and young solvers often lose track of which part is asked for.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
